claim: Enteroendocrine cells (EECs) are specialized sensory cells in the intestinal epithelium that sense and transduce nutrient information.
source: Enteroendocrine cells (EECs) are specialized sensory cells in the intestinal epithelium that sense and transduce nutrient information.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the function of EECs.

claim: High fat feeding alters EEC morphology.
source: Our results reveal that high fat feeding alters EEC morphology and converts them into a nutrient insensitive state that is coupled to endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: High fat feeding converts EECs into a nutrient insensitive state.
source: Our results reveal that high fat feeding alters EEC morphology and converts them into a nutrient insensitive state that is coupled to endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing reduced EEC calcium responses to nutrients after high fat feeding.

claim: High fat diet induced EEC changes are coupled to endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress.
source: Our results reveal that high fat feeding alters EEC morphology and converts them into a nutrient insensitive state that is coupled to endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data showing ER stress markers in EECs after high fat feeding.

claim: The novel adaptation of EECs to high fat feeding is called 'EEC silencing'.
source: We called this novel adaptation 'EEC silencing'.
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors for the phenomenon they observed.

claim: Germ-free zebrafish are resistant to high fat diet induced EEC silencing.
source: Gnotobiotic studies revealed that germ-free zebrafish are resistant to high fat diet induced EEC silencing.
evidence: This is a primary finding from gnotobiotic experiments comparing germ-free and conventionalized zebrafish.

claim: High fat feeding altered gut microbiota composition including enrichment of Acinetobacter bacteria.
source: High fat feeding altered gut microbiota composition including enrichment of Acinetobacter bacteria, and we identified an Acinetobacter strain sufficient to induce EEC silencing.
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing data showing changes in microbial community composition.

claim: An Acinetobacter strain is sufficient to induce EEC silencing.
source: High fat feeding altered gut microbiota composition including enrichment of Acinetobacter bacteria, and we identified an Acinetobacter strain sufficient to induce EEC silencing.
evidence: This is supported by monoassociation experiments showing that Acinetobacter sp. ZOR0008 alone can induce EEC morphological changes during high fat feeding.

claim: The transcription factor NeuroD1 plays an essential role to restrict intestinal progenitor cells to an EEC fate in mice.
source: Previous mouse studies have shown that the transcription factor NeuroD1 plays an essential role to restrict intestinal progenitor cells to an EEC fate (Li et al., 2011; Ray and Leiter, 2007), and is expressed in almost all EECs without expression in other intestinal epithelial cell lineages (Li et al., 2012; Ray et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous mouse studies.

claim: NeuroD1 is expressed in almost all EECs without expression in other intestinal epithelial cell lineages in mice.
source: Previous mouse studies have shown that the transcription factor NeuroD1 plays an essential role to restrict intestinal progenitor cells to an EEC fate (Li et al., 2011; Ray and Leiter, 2007), and is expressed in almost all EECs without expression in other intestinal epithelial cell lineages (Li et al., 2012; Ray et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous mouse studies.

claim: Neurod1+ cells in the zebrafish intestine label secretory but not absorptive cell lineages.
source: To further test whether these neurod1+ cells in the intestine label secretory but not absorptive cell lineages, we crossed Tg(neurod1:RFP) with the Notch reporter line Tg(tp1:EGFP) (Parsons et al., 2009). Activation of Notch signaling is essential to restrict intestinal progenitor cells to an absorptive cell fate (Crosnier et al., 2005; Li et al., 2012), suggesting tp1+ cells may represent enterocyte progenitors. In accord, we found that neurod1+ cells in the intestine do not overlap with tp1+ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no overlap between neurod1+ cells and tp1+ cells (Notch reporter) or fabp2+ cells (enterocyte marker).

claim: Neurod1+ cells in the zebrafish intestine do not overlap with the mature enterocyte marker ifabp/fabp2.
source: Additionally, our results demonstrated that neurod1+ cells in the intestine do not overlap with the mature enterocyte marker ifabp/fabp2 (Kanther et al., 2011) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing no overlap between neurod1+ cells and fabp2+ cells.

claim: Neurod1 expression in the zebrafish intestine occurs specifically in EECs.
source: These results suggested that, similar to mammals, neurod1 expression in the zebrafish intestine occurs specifically in EECs.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of experimental evidence showing neurod1+ cells express EEC markers and not markers of other cell types.

claim: EECs in the intestine are post-mitotic and require about 30 hr to differentiate from proliferating progenitors in zebrafish.
source: In addition, using EdU labeling in 5 dpf zebrafish larvae, we found that EECs in the intestine are post-mitotic and require about 30 hr to differentiate from proliferating progenitors (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by EdU tracing experiments showing the timing of EEC differentiation.

claim: PYY and CCK hormones are only expressed in EECs in the proximal intestine of zebrafish.
source: We found that PYY and CCK hormones, which are important for regulating fat digestion and feeding behavior, are only expressed in EECs in the proximal intestine where dietary fats and other nutrients are digested and absorbed (Carten et al., 2011; Farber et al., 2001) (Figure 1I–J).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence staining data showing regional expression patterns.

claim: Somatostatin expression occurred in EECs along the whole intestine of zebrafish.
source: In contrast, somatostatin expression occurred in EECs along the whole intestine and glucagon expressing EECs were found along the proximal and mid-intestine (segment 2) but excluded from the posterior intestine (segment 3) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing the distribution of somatostatin-expressing EECs.

claim: Glucagon expressing EECs were found along the proximal and mid-intestine (segment 2) but excluded from the posterior intestine (segment 3) in zebrafish.
source: In contrast, somatostatin expression occurred in EECs along the whole intestine and glucagon expressing EECs were found along the proximal and mid-intestine (segment 2) but excluded from the posterior intestine (segment 3) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing the distribution of glucagon-expressing EECs.

claim: The transient increase in intracellular calcium concentration is an important mediator and indicator of EEC function.
source: Therefore, the transient increase in intracellular calcium concentration is an important mediator and indicator of EEC function.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about EEC physiology and calcium signaling.

claim: Palmitate, but not the BSA vehicle control, activated a subset of EECs in zebrafish.
source: We found that palmitate, but not the BSA vehicle control, activated a subset of EECs (Figure 2B–F, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data showing EEC responses to palmitate stimulation.

claim: Similar patterns of EEC activation in the proximal intestine were induced by the fatty acids linoleate and dodecanoate in zebrafish.
source: Similar patterns of EEC activation in the proximal intestine were induced by the fatty acids linoleate and dodecanoate; whereas, the short chain fatty acid butyrate did not induce EEC activity (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data showing EEC responses to different fatty acids.

claim: The short chain fatty acid butyrate did not induce EEC activity in zebrafish.
source: Similar patterns of EEC activation in the proximal intestine were induced by the fatty acids linoleate and dodecanoate; whereas, the short chain fatty acid butyrate did not induce EEC activity (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data showing lack of EEC response to butyrate.

claim: The ability of EECs to respond to fatty acids is a conserved trait in zebrafish and mammalian EECs.
source: Our results further establish that activation by fatty acids is a conserved trait in zebrafish and mammalian EECs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that zebrafish EECs respond to fatty acids, similar to what has been observed in mammals.

claim: The ability of EECs in the proximal intestine to respond to palmitate stimulation was quickly and significantly reduced after 6 hr of HF meal feeding in zebrafish.
source: To our surprise, we found that the ability of EECs in the proximal intestine to respond to palmitate stimulation in our EEC activity assay was quickly and significantly reduced after 6 hr of HF meal feeding (Figure 2H–J, Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data comparing EEC responses before and after high fat feeding.

claim: Glucose stimulation activated EECs only in the proximal intestine of the zebrafish under unfed control conditions.
source: First, we investigated EEC responses to glucose stimulation. Similar to fatty acids, glucose stimulation activated EECs only in the proximal intestine of the zebrafish under unfed control conditions (Figure 3A and B, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data showing regional specificity of glucose-induced EEC activation.

claim: Glucose-stimulated elevation of intracellular calcium concentrations and hormone secretion in EECs is dependent upon the EEC sodium dependent glucose cotransporter 1 (Sglt1) in mammalian cell culture studies.
source: Previous mammalian cell culture studies reported that glucose-stimulated elevation of intracellular calcium concentrations and hormone secretion in EECs is dependent upon the EEC sodium dependent glucose cotransporter 1 (Sglt1), an apical membrane protein that is expressed in small intestine and renal tubules and actively transports glucose and galactose into cells (Song et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous mammalian study.

claim: Sglt1 is expressed on the apical surface of zebrafish intestinal epithelial cells including enterocytes and EECs.
source: Similarly, we found that Sglt1 is expressed on the apical surface of zebrafish intestinal epithelial cells including enterocytes and EECs (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence staining data showing Sglt1 localization.

claim: Co-stimulation with glucose and phlorizin, a chemical inhibitor of Sglt1, blocked the EEC activation induced by glucose in zebrafish.
source: In addition, co-stimulation with glucose and phlorizin, a chemical inhibitor of Sglt1, blocked the EEC activation induced by glucose (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data showing that Sglt1 inhibition prevents glucose-induced EEC activation.

claim: The EEC response to glucose stimulation was significantly increased by the addition of NaCl in the stimulant solution in zebrafish.
source: Consistently, the EEC response to glucose stimulation was significantly increased by the addition of NaCl in the stimulant solution which will facilate sodium gradient dependent glucose transport by Sglt1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data showing enhanced EEC responses with NaCl addition.

claim: Zebrafish EECs responded to the Sglt1 substrate galactose, but not fructose.
source: In addition, zebrafish EECs also responded to the other Sglt1 substrate, galactose, but not fructose (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data showing differential EEC responses to different sugars.

claim: Glucose can induce EEC activity in a Sglt1 dependent manner in the zebrafish intestine.
source: These results suggest that glucose can induce EEC activity in a Sglt1 dependent manner in the zebrafish intestine.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including Sglt1 expression, inhibitor studies, and substrate specificity.

claim: HF feeding significantly reduced EECs' response to subsequent glucose stimulation in zebrafish.
source: Indeed, HF feeding significantly reduced EECs' response to subsequent glucose stimulation (Figure 3H–J, Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data comparing glucose responses before and after high fat feeding.

claim: Zebrafish EECs that responded to cysteine were located primarily in the mid intestine.
source: However, in contrast to the fatty acid and glucose responses, zebrafish EECs that responded to cysteine were located primarily in the mid intestine (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B) and HF meal ingestion did not significantly impair subsequent EEC responses to cysteine (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data showing regional specificity of cysteine-responsive EECs.

claim: HF meal ingestion did not significantly impair subsequent EEC responses to cysteine in zebrafish.
source: However, in contrast to the fatty acid and glucose responses, zebrafish EECs that responded to cysteine were located primarily in the mid intestine (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B) and HF meal ingestion did not significantly impair subsequent EEC responses to cysteine (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data showing maintained cysteine responses after high fat feeding.

claim: HF feeding impairs the function of palmitate and glucose responsive EECs in the proximal intestine, the region where fat absorption takes place in zebrafish.
source: These results collectively indicate that HF feeding impairs the function of palmitate and glucose responsive EECs in the proximal intestine, the region where fat absorption takes place.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental observations about regional and nutrient-specific effects of high fat feeding.

claim: Most EECs in zebrafish under control conditions are in an open-type morphology with an apical process that extends to the intestinal lumen.
source: In zebrafish under control conditions, most EECs are in an open-type morphology (Figure 1B–G) with an apical process that extends to the intestinal lumen, allowing them to directly interact with the contents of the intestinal lumen (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data showing EEC morphology.

claim: Most EECs in the proximal zebrafish intestine had adopted a closed-type morphology after 6 hr of HF feeding.
source: When we examined the proximal zebrafish intestine after 6 hr of HF feeding, we discovered that most EECs had adopted a closed-type morphology that apparently lacked an apical extension and no longer had access to the lumenal contents (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data showing changes in EEC morphology after high fat feeding.

claim: The striking change in EEC morphology during HF feeding is not due to EEC turnover nor EEC apoptosis but is instead due to adaptation of the existing EECs.
source: These results suggest that the striking change in EEC morphology during HF feeding is not due to EEC turnover nor EEC apoptosis but is instead due to adaptation of the existing EECs.
evidence: This is supported by photoconversion tracing experiments and apoptosis assays showing no new EEC generation or cell death.

claim: The EEC morphology score gradually decreased upon HF feeding in zebrafish.
source: We found that the EEC morphology score gradually decreased upon HFfeeding (Figure 4E, Video 5), indicating that EECs had changed from an open-type to closed-type morphology.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of EEC morphology over time during high fat feeding.

claim: EEC apical processes undergo dynamic retraction after HF feeding in zebrafish.
source: Using in vivo confocal time-lapse imaging in Tg(neurod1:lifeAct-EGFP) zebrafish, we confirmed that EEC apical processes undergo dynamic retraction after HF feeding (Figure 4F), which was not observed in control animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C and D, Video 6).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data showing the dynamics of EEC morphological changes.

claim: EECs in the distal-intestine retained their open-type morphology following HF feeding in zebrafish.
source: Interestingly, EECs in the distal-intestine retained their open-type morphology following HF feeding (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–H), suggesting the adaptation from open- to closed-type EEC morphology is a specific response of EECs in the proximal intestine.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing regional differences in EEC responses to high fat feeding.

claim: The diet-induced EEC morphology change occurs in adult zebrafish.
source: Our results demonstrated that, consistent with our observations in larvae zebrafish, 10 hr HF feeding triggered a similar open- to closed-type change in EEC morphology in adult zebrafish proximal intestine (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data from adult zebrafish showing similar morphological changes as in larvae.

claim: Diet-induced EEC adaptation is not restricted to larval stage animals but is a general postprandial physiological response.
source: This suggests that this diet-induced EEC adaptation is not restricted to larval stage animals but is a general postprandial physiological response.
evidence: This is inferred from observations in both larval and adult zebrafish showing similar responses.

claim: EECs' calcium response to palmitate paralleled the clearance of the HF meal from the intestine in zebrafish.
source: We observed that EECs' calcium response to palmitate paralleled the clearance of the HF meal from the intestine (Figure 5A,B and G).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data at different time points during recovery from high fat feeding.

claim: Twenty hours after HF feeding, intestinal fat was almost completely cleared from the intestine and the EEC calcium response to palmitate was restored comparable to that of unfed controls in zebrafish.
source: Twenty hours after HF feeding, intestinal fat was almost completely cleared from the intestine and the EEC calcium response to palmitate was restored comparable to that of unfed controls (Figure 5B and H).
evidence: This is supported by imaging and calcium response data showing recovery of EEC function.

claim: After 20 hr of recovery from HF feeding, the apical extension of most EECs had returned to the intestinal lumen and the EEC morphology score normalized in zebrafish.
source: HF feeding-induced changes in EEC morphology was also reversible. After 20 hr of recovery from HF feeding, the apical extension of most EECs had returned to the intestinal lumen and the EEC morphology score normalized (Figure 5C–F and I).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing restoration of EEC morphology after recovery.

claim: Restoration of EEC functional and morphological features after high fat feeding was due to recovery of existing EECs rather than new EEC neogenesis in zebrafish.
source: To investigate whether restoration of these functional and morphological features was due to recovery of existing EECs or new EEC neogenesis, we performed similar Kaede photoconvertable EEC cell tracing using the Tg(neurod1:Gal4); Tg(UAS:Kaede) system (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The existing EECs were labeled with UV after 6 hr of HF feeding. Following the photolabeling of EECs, the zebrafish were transferred to fresh egg water and intestines were imaged 20 hr after recovery. Almost all EECs in the recovered zebrafish were labeled with red Kaede (Figure 5J–K) indicating that HF feeding did not induce EEC apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by photoconversion tracing experiments showing that pre-existing EECs recover rather than being replaced by new cells.

claim: EECs' morphological and functional adaptations in response to HF feeding are transient and reversible in zebrafish.
source: In summary, our data suggest that EECs' morphological and functional adaptations in response to HF feeding are transient and reversible.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on recovery experiments showing restoration of EEC function and morphology.

claim: HF feeding led to broad increases in expression of transcripts encoding EEC hormones in zebrafish.
source: Quantitative RT-PCR assays in dissected zebrafish digestive tracts 6 hr after HF feeding revealed broad increases in expression of transcripts encoding EEC hormones (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data showing increased hormone transcript levels.

claim: The largest increases in EEC hormone transcript levels after HF feeding were pyyb and ccka in zebrafish.
source: The largest increases were pyyb and ccka (Figure 6A), both of which are expressed by EECs in the proximal zebrafish intestine (Figure 1) and are important for the response to dietary lipid.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data showing fold changes in transcript levels.

claim: HF feeding did not significantly alter expression of EEC specific transcription factors (neurod1, pax6b, isl1) in zebrafish.
source: However, HF feeding did not significantly alter expression of EEC specific transcription factors (neurod1, pax6b, isl1), nor the total number of EECs per animal (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR and cell counting data.

claim: HF feeding did not significantly alter the total number of EECs per animal in zebrafish.
source: However, HF feeding did not significantly alter expression of EEC specific transcription factors (neurod1, pax6b, isl1), nor the total number of EECs per animal (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data.

claim: HF feeding led to gradual increases in ccka and pyyb transcript levels which plateaued 6 hr after HF feeding in zebrafish.
source: We found that HF feeding led to gradual increases in ccka and pyyb transcript levelss which plateaued 6 hr after HF feeding (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by time-course qRT-PCR data.

claim: PYY immunofluorescence revealed reduced fluorescence intensity at 5 hr and 8 hr post HF fed zebrafish compared to control zebrafish.
source: Despite these increases in transcript level, PYY immunofluorescence revealed that reduced fluorescence intensity at 5 hr and 8 hr post HF fed zebrafish compared to control zebrafish (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D and F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data.

claim: HF feeding increased expression of UPR genes including chaperone proteins Gpr94 and Bip as early as 2 hr after HF feeding in zebrafish.
source: Using quantitative RT-PCR analysis in dissected zebrafish digestive tracts, we found that HF feeding increased expression of UPR genes including chaperone proteins Gpr94 and Bip as early as 2 hr after HF feeding (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data showing increased ER stress marker expression.

claim: Zebrafish larvae fed a HF meal, but not control larvae, displayed a significant induction of GFP in neurod1+ EECs in the Tg(ef1α:xbp1δ-gfp) reporter line.
source: We crossed Tg(ef1α:xbp1δ-gfp) with Tg(neurod1:RFP) zebrafish and found that zebrafish larvae fed a HF meal, but not control larvae, displayed a significant induction of GFP in neurod1+ EECs (Figure 6L–N; Videos 7 and 8).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data using an ER stress reporter showing activation in EECs after high fat feeding.

claim: Treatment with TUDCA, an ER stress inhibitor, prevented HF feeding from reducing the EEC morphology score in zebrafish.
source: Whereas HF feeding normally reduces the EEC morphology score, this did not occur in zebrafish treated with tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA), a known ER stress inhibitor (Uppala et al., 2017; Vang et al., 2014) (Figure 6O–Q).
evidence: This is supported by morphology quantification data in TUDCA-treated animals.

claim: Thapsigargin treatment reduced the EEC calcium response to both glucose and palmitate in zebrafish.
source: Thapsigargin treatment, however, reduced the EEC calcium response in that region to both glucose and palmitate (Figure 6D–I, Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–E) and decreased the EEC morphology score, both key phenomena associated with EEC silencing (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging and morphology data in thapsigargin-treated animals.

claim: Treatment with brefeldin A (BFA), an ER stress inducer, significantly decreased the EEC morphology score in zebrafish.
source: To confirm this result, we tested a second ER stress inducer brefeldin A (BFA), which inhibits anterograde ER export to Golgi and blocks protein secretion (Donaldson et al., 1992; Klausner et al., 1992). Similar to thapsigargin, treatment with BFA significantly decreased the EEC morphology score (Figure 6K).
evidence: This is supported by morphology quantification data in BFA-treated animals.

claim: Increased hormone synthesis and secretion following HF feeding induce ER stress in EECs which leads to EEC silencing.
source: These results support a working model wherein increased hormone synthesis and secretion following HF feeding induce ER stress in EECs which leads to EEC silencing.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on multiple lines of experimental evidence linking ER stress to EEC silencing.

claim: Treatment of Tg(neurod1:Gcamp6f) zebrafish with orlistat during HF feeding significantly increased the ability of EECs to subsequently respond to glucose and palmitate.
source: We found that treatment of Tg(neurod1:Gcamp6f) zebrafish with orlistat during HF feeding significantly increased the ability of EECs to subsequently respond to glucose and palmitate (Figure 7A–F).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data comparing orlistat-treated and untreated animals during high fat feeding.

claim: Treatment with orlistat prevented HF induced EEC morphological changes in zebrafish.
source: We found that following 10 hr of HF feeding, EECs in control animals had switched from an open-type to a closed-type morphology and significantly reduced the EEC morphology score (Figure 7G and N). By contrast, treatment with orlistat prevented HF induced EEC morphological changes (Figure 7H and N), suggesting lipase activity is required for EEC silencing.
evidence: This is supported by morphology quantification data in orlistat-treated animals.

claim: Lipase activity is required for EEC silencing in zebrafish.
source: By contrast, treatment with orlistat prevented HF induced EEC morphological changes (Figure 7H and N), suggesting lipase activity is required for EEC silencing.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that lipase inhibition prevents EEC silencing.

claim: Orlistat treatment significantly reduced the percentage of EECs that are ef1α:xbp1δ-gfp+ following HF feeding in zebrafish.
source: We found that orlistat treatment significantly reduced the percentage of EECs that are ef1α:xbp1δ-gfp+ following HF feeding (Figure 7I,J and O).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of ER stress reporter activation in orlistat-treated animals.

claim: HF feeding significantly increased the number of NF-κB+ EECs in zebrafish.
source: After crossing a transgenic reporter of NF-κB activity Tg(NFkB:EGFP) (Kanther et al., 2011) with Tg(neurod1:RFP), we found that HF feeding significantly increased the number of NF-κB+ EECs (Figure 7K and P), but that this effect could be significantly reduced by treatment with orlistat or the ER stress inhibitor TUDCA (Figure 7L,M and P).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of NF-κB reporter activation in EECs.

claim: Treatment with orlistat or TUDCA significantly reduced HF feeding-induced NF-κB activation in EECs in zebrafish.
source: After crossing a transgenic reporter of NF-κB activity Tg(NFkB:EGFP) (Kanther et al., 2011) with Tg(neurod1:RFP), we found that HF feeding significantly increased the number of NF-κB+ EECs (Figure 7K and P), but that this effect could be significantly reduced by treatment with orlistat or the ER stress inhibitor TUDCA (Figure 7L,M and P).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of NF-κB reporter activation in treated animals.

claim: EEC silencing and associated signaling events that follow ingestion of a HF meal require lipase activity in zebrafish.
source: These results indicate that EEC silencing and associated signaling events that follow ingestion of a HF meal require lipase activity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on orlistat experiments showing that lipase inhibition prevents multiple aspects of EEC silencing.

claim: Treatment with palmitate for 6 hr significantly reduced the ability of EECs to respond to subsequent palmitate stimulation in zebrafish.
source: Treatment with palmitate for 6 hr significantly reduced the ability of EECs to respond to subsequent palmitate stimulation, but did not influence the EEC morphology score, nor the EEC response toward subsequent glucose stimulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging and morphology data in palmitate-treated animals.

claim: Palmitate treatment did not influence the EEC morphology score in zebrafish.
source: Treatment with palmitate for 6 hr significantly reduced the ability of EECs to respond to subsequent palmitate stimulation, but did not influence the EEC morphology score, nor the EEC response toward subsequent glucose stimulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is supported by morphology quantification data in palmitate-treated animals.

claim: Palmitate treatment did not influence the EEC response toward subsequent glucose stimulation in zebrafish.
source: Treatment with palmitate for 6 hr significantly reduced the ability of EECs to respond to subsequent palmitate stimulation, but did not influence the EEC morphology score, nor the EEC response toward subsequent glucose stimulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in palmitate-treated animals.

claim: Palmitate treatment did not induce significant ER stress activation like HF feeding in zebrafish.
source: Similary, using Tg(ef1α:xbp1δ-gfp) and real-time PCR to examine relative bip and grp94 expression, we found that palmitate treatment did not induce significant ER stress activation like HF feeding (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This is supported by ER stress reporter imaging and qRT-PCR data in palmitate-treated animals.

claim: The fatty acid palmitate is sufficient to induce only a portion of the EEC silencing phenotype induced by a complex HF meal in zebrafish.
source: These results suggest that the fatty acid palmitate is sufficient to induce only a portion of the EEC silencing phenotype induced by a complex HF meal.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on comparing effects of palmitate treatment versus complex high fat meal.

claim: In the absence of HF feeding, there were no significant differences between GF and CV zebrafish in their EEC morphology score or EEC response to palmitate.
source: In the absence of HF feeding, we observed no significant differences between GF and CV zebrafish in their EEC morphology score or EEC response to palmitate (Figure 8C,D,G and I).
evidence: This is supported by morphology and calcium imaging data comparing germ-free and conventionalized animals under control conditions.

claim: EECs in GF zebrafish did not show a change in morphology after HF feeding, in contrast to CV HF-fed zebrafish larvae.
source: In contrast to CV HF-fed zebrafish larvae, EECs in GF zebrafish did not show a change in morphology after HF feeding (Figure 8A,B and I) and exhibited significantly greater responses to palmitate stimulation (Figure 8E,F and H).
evidence: This is supported by morphology quantification data comparing germ-free and conventionalized animals after high fat feeding.

claim: EECs in GF zebrafish exhibited significantly greater responses to palmitate stimulation after HF feeding compared to CV zebrafish.
source: In contrast to CV HF-fed zebrafish larvae, EECs in GF zebrafish did not show a change in morphology after HF feeding (Figure 8A,B and I) and exhibited significantly greater responses to palmitate stimulation (Figure 8E,F and H).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data comparing germ-free and conventionalized animals after high fat feeding.

claim: The ability of HF feeding to induce reporters of ER stress and NF-κB activation was significantly reduced in GF compared to CV zebrafish.
source: In accord, the ability of HF feeding to induce reporters of ER stress and NF-κB activation was significantly reduced in GF compared to CV zebrafish (Figure 8J and K).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of ER stress and NF-κB reporter activation in germ-free versus conventionalized animals.

claim: Colonization by microbiota mediates EEC silencing in HF fed zebrafish.
source: These results indicate that colonization by microbiota mediates EEC silencing in HF fed zebrafish.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on gnotobiotic experiments showing that germ-free animals are resistant to EEC silencing.

claim: EECs' response to palmitate after HF feeding in myd88 mutant zebrafish was equivalent to that of wild type fish.
source: To test if EEC silencing requires TLR signaling, we evaluated myd88 mutant zebrafish (Burns et al., 2017). We found that EECs' response to palmitate after HF feeding was equivalent to that of wild type fish (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), suggesting microbiota promote EEC silencing in a Myd88-independent manner.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in myd88 mutant animals.

claim: Microbiota promote EEC silencing in a Myd88-independent manner in zebrafish.
source: We found that EECs' response to palmitate after HF feeding was equivalent to that of wild type fish (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), suggesting microbiota promote EEC silencing in a Myd88-independent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that myd88 mutants show normal EEC silencing.

claim: Intestinal microbiota abundance had increased ~20 fold following 6 hr of HF feeding in zebrafish.
source: Strikingly, we found that intestinal microbiota abundance had increased ~20 fold following 6 hr of HF feeding (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by CFU analysis data.

claim: HF feeding had a relatively smaller but consistent effect on overall bacterial community structure in both gut and media in zebrafish.
source: The addition of HF feeding had a relatively smaller but consistent effect on overall bacterial community structure in both gut and media (PERMANOVA p=0.2 control gut vs HF gut, p=0.094 control media vs HF media) (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and statistical analysis of bacterial community structure.

claim: HF feeding caused a small reduction in within-sample diversity among media microbiotas as measured by Faith's Phylogenetic Diversity in zebrafish.
source: HF feeding caused a small reduction in within-sample diversity among media microbiotas as measured by Faith's Phylogenetic Diversity (Kruskal-Wallis p=0.049), but no significant effects on gut microbiotas (p=0.29) (Faith and Baker, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by alpha diversity analysis of 16S rRNA gene sequencing data.

claim: HF feeding markedly decreased the relative abundance of members of class Betaproteobacteria in zebrafish media.
source: Members of class Betaproteobacteria dominated the control media, but HF feeding markedly decreased their relative abundance (LDA effect size 5.45, p=0.049).
evidence: This is supported by taxonomic analysis of 16S rRNA gene sequencing data.

claim: HF feeding increased the relative abundance of members of class Gammaproteobacteria in zebrafish media.
source: Conversely, HF feeding increased the relative abundance of members of class Gammaproteobacteria (LDA effect size 5.49, p=0.049; Figure 9D) such as genera Acinetobacter (LDA effect size 5.13, p=0.049), Pseudomonas (LDA effect size 5.02, p=0.049) and Aeromonas (LDA effect size 4.78, p=0.049; Figure 9F; Supplementary file 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by taxonomic analysis of 16S rRNA gene sequencing data.

claim: HF feeding increased the relative abundance of class Cytophagia from phylum Bacteroidetes in zebrafish media.
source: HF feeding also increased the relative abundance in media of class Cytophagia from phylum Bacteroidetes (LDA effect size 4.66, p=0.049; Figure 9D) due to increases in the genus Flectobacillus (LDA effect size 4.76, p=0.049; Figure 9E; Supplementary file 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by taxonomic analysis of 16S rRNA gene sequencing data.

claim: HF feeding significantly increased abundance of class Cytophagia in zebrafish gut.
source: However, similar to the media, HF feeding significantly increased abundance of class Cytophagia (LDA effect size 4.01, p=0.018; Figure 9D) due to enrichment of Flectobacillus (LDA effect size 4.01, p=0.004; Figure 9F).
evidence: This is supported by taxonomic analysis of 16S rRNA gene sequencing data from gut samples.

claim: HF feeding resulted in a 100-fold increase in the relative abundance of Acinetobacter sp. in the zebrafish gut.
source: Additionally, HF feeding resulted in a 100-fold increase the relative abundance of Acinetobacter sp. in the gut (average 0.04% in control gut, 4.28% in HF gut; LDA effect size 4.31, p=0.001; Figure 9G, Supplementary file 2 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by taxonomic analysis of 16S rRNA gene sequencing data from gut samples.

claim: Only Acinetobacter sp. ZOR0008 was sufficient to significantly reduce the EEC morphology score upon HF feeding in monoassociated zebrafish.
source: Strikingly, only Acinetobacter sp. ZOR0008 was sufficient to significantly reduce the EEC morphology score upon HF feeding (Figure 9J) similar to conventionalized animals (Figure 8A,B and I).
evidence: This is supported by morphology quantification data from monoassociation experiments.

claim: Monoassociation with Acinetobacter sp. ZOR0008 alone is sufficient to reduce EEC calcium response to palmitate stimulation following HF feeding compared with GF controls in zebrafish.
source: Consistently, we also found that monoassociation with Acinetobacter sp. ZOR0008 alone is sufficient to reduce EEC calcium response to palmitate stimulation following HF feeding compared with GF controls (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data from monoassociation experiments.

claim: The effects of microbiota on EEC silencing following HF feeding display strong bacterial species specificity in zebrafish.
source: These results indicate that the effects of microbiota on EEC silencing following HF feeding display strong bacterial species specificity, and suggest Acinetobacter bacteria enriched by HF feeding may mediate the effect of microbiota on HF sensing by EECs.
evidence: This is inferred from monoassociation experiments showing that only one of multiple tested bacterial strains could induce EEC silencing.

claim: Treatment with NAC or L-NAME did not prevent HF feeding induced EEC silencing in zebrafish.
source: We first treated conventional raised zebrafish with known ROS scavengers N-acetylcysteine (NAC) (Mocelin et al., 2019) and N(ω)-nitro-L-arginine methyl ester (L-NAME) that can inhibit host reactive nitrogen species production (Bradley et al., 2010), however neither of these compounds prevented HF feeding induced EEC silencing (Figure 9—figure supplement 3A–D and G).
evidence: This is supported by morphology quantification data in NAC and L-NAME treated animals.

claim: No significant differences in intestinal fluorescence were detected in the conditions of GF, CV and Acinetobacter sp. monoassociated zebrafish with or without HF feeding using the ROS indicator CM-H2DCFDA.
source: Using a general oxidative stress chemical indicator CM-H2DCFDA whose fluorescence can be induced by ROS mediated oxidation, we also failed to detect significant differences in intestinal fluoresence in the conditions of GF, CV and Acinetobacter sp. monoassociated zebrafish with or without HF feeding (Figure 9—figure supplement 3E–F and H).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence quantification data using a ROS indicator.

claim: No significant induction of ROS production was observed in in vitro cultures of Aeromonas sp. and Acinetobacter sp. in media containing HF meal.
source: Similarly we did not observe significant induction of ROS production in in vitro cultures of Aeromonas sp. and Acinetobacter sp. in media containing HF meal (Figure 9—figure supplement 3I).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro ROS measurement data.

claim: Microbiota dependent EEC silencing following HF feeding is not mediated by ROS signaling in zebrafish.
source: These results suggest that microbiota dependent EEC silencing following HF feeding is not mediated by ROS signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of evidence showing that ROS inhibition or measurement does not correlate with EEC silencing.

claim: EEC silencing is a physiologically relevant postprandial adaptation, rather than acute toxicity in EECs stimulated by high fat feeding.
source: This together with other data presented here indicate that EEC silencing is a physiologically relevant postprandial adaptation, rather than acute toxicity in EECs stimulated by high fat feeding.
evidence: This is inferred from the reversibility of EEC silencing and lack of cell death.

claim: EEC silencing is a response that EECs display following consumption of a high fat meal only in the presence of specific microbes.
source: Our evidence further suggests that EEC silencing is a response that EECs display following consumption of a high fat meal only in the presence of specific microbes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on gnotobiotic and monoassociation experiments.

claim: High fat feeding reduces intestinal glucose sensing and glucose induced GLP-1 secretion in vivo in mice.
source: The observation that EECs exhibited reduced sensitivity to oral glucose following high fat feeding is interesting and consistent with the finding in mice that high fat feeding reduces intestinal glucose sensing and glucose induced GLP-1 secretion in vivo (Bauer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous mouse study.

claim: Small intestinal cultures from high fat fed mice exhibit reduced secretory responsiveness to nutrient stimuli including glucose when compared with cultures from control mice.
source: In vitro, small intestinal cultures from high fat fed mice also exhibit reduced secretory responsiveness to nutrient stimuli including glucose when compared with cultures from control mice (Richards et al., 2016) but underlying mechanisms remained unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous mouse study.

claim: The majority of EECs in the intestinal tract are open with an apical extension and microvilli facing the intestinal lumen.
source: The majority of EECs in the intestinal tract are open with an apical extension and microvilli facing the intestinal lumen.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about EEC morphology.

claim: Some EECs lie flat on the basement membrane and are 'closed' to the gut lumen.
source: In contrast, some EECs lie flat on the basement membrane and are 'closed' to the gut lumen (Gribble and Reimann, 2016).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about EEC morphology, supported by citation.

claim: The presence of open and closed EECs has been observed in both mammals and fish.
source: The presence of open and closed EECs has been observed in both mammals and fish (Rombout et al., 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: It was previously believed that the open and closed EECs were two differentiated EEC types that perhaps had different physiological functions.
source: Previously, it was believed that the open and closed EECs were two differentiated EEC types that perhaps had different physiological functions (Gribble and Reimann, 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about previous understanding in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Individual EECs can convert reversibly from an open to a closed state.
source: However, our data reveal that individual EECs can convert reversibly from an open to a closed state.
evidence: This is a novel finding from the current study based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: EECs possess plasticity to actively prune their apical extensions.
source: This indicates that EECs possess plasticity to actively prune their apical extensions.
evidence: This is inferred from observations of reversible morphological changes in EECs.

claim: Sensory neurons can eliminate their dendrites and axons during development and in response to injury through active pruning.
source: Studies from multiple organisms revealed that sensory neurons can eliminate their dendrites and axons during development and in response to injury through active pruning (Kanamori et al., 2013; Nikolaev et al., 2009; Sagasti et al., 2005; Williams et al., 2006; Yu and Schuldiner, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on neuronal pruning.

claim: EECs possess many neuron-like features including neurotransmitters, neurofilaments, and synaptic proteins.
source: It is well known that EECs possess many neuron-like features including neurotransmitters, neurofilaments, and synaptic proteins (Bohórquez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about EEC characteristics, supported by citation.

claim: Blocking fat digestion and subsequent lipid absorption through orlistat treatment prevented EEC silencing after high fat feeding in zebrafish.
source: Blocking fat digestion and subsequent lipid absorption through orlistat treatment prevented EEC silencing after high fat feeding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that orlistat prevents EEC morphological and functional changes.

claim: Repeated or continuous stimulation of G-protein coupled receptors (GPCR) like free fatty acid receptors induces GPCR desensitation through receptor internalization into vesicles, degradation in lysosomes, and decreased receptor mRNA levels.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that repeated or continuous stimulation of G-protein coupled receptors (GPCR) like free fatty acid receptors induces GPCR desensitation through receptor internalization into vesicles, degradation in lysosomes, and decreased receptor mRNA levels (Rajagopal and Shenoy, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on GPCR desensitization.

claim: ER stress markers are evident in EECs within 2 hr after high fat feeding in zebrafish.
source: We find that ER stress markers are evident in EECs within 2 hr after high fat feeding, concomitant with increased hormone transcription, whereas EEC silencing is not established until 6 hr.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR and reporter imaging data showing timing of ER stress activation.

claim: The continuous ER stress which is induced throughout the high fat feeding as early as 2 hr appears to be a key mechanism leading to the later EEC silencing response.
source: The continuous ER stress which is induced throughout the high fat feeding as early as 2 hr appears to be a key mechanism leading to the later EEC silencing response.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal relationship between ER stress activation and EEC silencing.

claim: EECs are surrounded by absorptive enterocytes and these two cell types exhibit complex bi-directional communication.
source: Within the intestinal epithelium, EECs are surrounded by absorptive enterocytes and these two cell types exhibit complex bi-directional communication (Hein et al., 2013; Hsieh et al., 2009; Okawa et al., 2009; Shimotoyodome et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on EEC-enterocyte interactions.

claim: Dietary manipulations and changes in gut microbiota have been shown to affect EEC cell number and GI hormone gene expression in mice and zebrafish.
source: Dietary manipulations and changes in gut microbiota have been shown to affect EEC cell number and GI hormone gene expression in mice and zebrafish (Arora et al., 2018; Rawls et al., 2004; Richards et al., 2016; Troll et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In mice, microbiota colonization reduced expression of genes associated with synaptic cycling, ER stress response and cell polarity in GLP-1 secreting EECs.
source: In mice, microbiota colonization reduced expression of genes associated with synaptic cycling, ER stress response and cell polarity in GLP-1 secreting EECs (Arora et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous mouse study.

claim: Lipid digestion and absorption is impaired in germ-free animals in zebrafish and mice.
source: Previous studies in gnotobiotic zebrafish and mice have shown that lipid digestion and absorption is impaired in germ-free animals and enterocytes in germ-free conditions exhibit reduced lipid droplet accumulation (Martinez-Guryn et al., 2018; Semova et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous gnotobiotic studies.

claim: Acinetobacter was the most highly enriched genus in the larval zebrafish intestine following high fat feeding in this study.
source: Acinetobacter was the most highly enriched genus in the larval zebrafish intestine following high fat feeding in this study and was also enriched in adult zebrafish gut following a chronic high fat diet (Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing data from the current study and citation to a previous study.

claim: Acinetobacter was enriched in adult zebrafish gut following a chronic high fat diet.
source: Acinetobacter was the most highly enriched genus in the larval zebrafish intestine following high fat feeding in this study and was also enriched in adult zebrafish gut following a chronic high fat diet (Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A. baumannii, a related oportunitistic pathogen, can signal to host epithelial cells through secreted outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) and activation of downstream inflammatory pathways.
source: Studies suggest that A. baumannii, a related oportunitistic pathogen, can signal to host epithelial cells through secreted outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) and activation of downstream inflammatory pathways (Jha et al., 2017; Jin et al., 2011; Jun et al., 2013; March et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on A. baumannii.

claim: Acinetobacter strains are known to secrete phospholipase that can affect host cell membrane stability and interfere with host signaling.
source: In addition to OMVs, Acinetobacter strains are known to secrete phospholipase that can affect host cell membrane stability and interfere with host signaling (Lee et al., 2017; Songer, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on Acinetobacter.

claim: Members of the Acinetobacter genus are known to possess potent oil degrading and lipolytic activities.
source: Members of the Acinetobacter genus are also known to possess potent oil degrading and lipolytic activities (Lal and Khanna, 1996; Snellman and Colwell, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on Acinetobacter.

claim: Species from Acinetobacter genus have the ability to produce emulsifiers which might enhance lipid digestion.
source: Moreover, species from Acinetobacter genus have the ability to produce emulsifiers which might enhance lipid digestion (Navon-Venezia et al., 1995; Toren et al., 2001; Walzer et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on Acinetobacter, with speculation about potential effects on lipid digestion.

claim: Acinetobacter spp. in the human gut are positively associated with plasma triglycerides and total- and LDL-cholesterol.
source: Acinetobacter spp. in the human gut are positively associated with plasma triglycerides and total- and LDL-cholesterol (Graessler et al., 2013), and Acinetobacter spp. are also enriched in the crypts of the small intestine and colon in mammals (Mao et al., 2015; Pédron et al., 2012; Saffarian et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous human and mammalian studies.

claim: Acinetobacter spp. are enriched in the crypts of the small intestine and colon in mammals.
source: Acinetobacter spp. in the human gut are positively associated with plasma triglycerides and total- and LDL-cholesterol (Graessler et al., 2013), and Acinetobacter spp. are also enriched in the crypts of the small intestine and colon in mammals (Mao et al., 2015; Pédron et al., 2012; Saffarian et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous mammalian studies.
